Title: Mycoponically Integrated Network Device for Multimodal Sensing with Living Mycelial Networks
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
Physical Sciences — Engineering
Mycoponically Integrated Network Device for Multimodal Sensing with
Living Mycelial Networks
Zihan Oliver Zenga, David Marshall Porterfieldb, and Upinder Kaurb,1
This manuscript was compiled on April 28, 2026
Multimodal environmental monitoring conventionally requires a
suite of purpose-built transducers, each constrained to a predefined
target.
Here,
we present MIND (Mycoponically Integrated
Network Device), a platform that sustains living fungal mycelial
networks on porous bioceramic substrates and reads their passive
extracellular voltages.
Without hardware modification, a single
device produces distinguishable bioelectrical responses to 14 stimuli
spanning chemical, optical, mechanical, thermal, and biological
domains. We show that steady-state intensity responses follow Hill-
type calibration functions conserved across five phylogenetically
diverse fungal species, and that multichannel decoding recovers
stimulus duration, spatial origin, and continuous position from
the bioelectrical output. Strain selection tunes sensitivity without
hardware redesign. The platform restores full electrophysiological
function within 72 h of mechanical damage and has maintained
calibration-quality readout for more than 11 months of continuous
operation.
These results position fungal electrophysiology as a
measurement platform for sensing applications in which the full
stimulus set, the electrode geometry, and the recovery requirements
cannot be fully specified in advance.

Conventional sensors are typically engineered for defined targets or operating
regimes. Monitoring chemical, optical, mechanical, and thermal domains often
requires a suite of distinct transducers, whereas fungal-based biosensing can
potentiate broader biosensing spectra. Metabolically active hyphae form an
electrically coupled mycelial lattice in which local ionic perturbations propagate
electrophysiologically as distributed extracellular voltage transients (1, 2).
Photoreceptors, ion channels, chemosensory proteins, and mechanosensors
each couple into the same membrane-voltage electrophysiological transduction
pathway through ligand-specific membrane receptors, often involving calcium
channels (3–6). This organization allows a single mycelial network to integrate
cellular control across multiple physical and biological domains.
Empirical work has shown that living mycelia generate measurable electrical
responses to the physical and chemical environment and can support biohybrid
actuation (7–9). These data are usually reported as qualitative correlations
between an input stimulus and the voltage patterns. Complex information
such as stimulus location, intensity, duration, or simultaneous stimuli from the
bioelectric signal remains unresolved (1, 2, 10). Quantitative applications of
fungal electrophysiology (sensing, robotics, computation) therefore require a
robust, integrative architecture that preserves metabolic activity, standardizes
electrode coupling, and yields signals sufficiently stable for calibration.
Existing approaches relying on Petri-dish or bag-cultured substrates cannot
sustain the metabolic activity required for long-duration sensing. Dried or
thermally inactivated mycelial substrates can function in limited applications as
bioelectronic materials, but not as living electrophysiological biosensors through
transduction of cellular receptors (11–13). The agar/Petri-dish culture method
can demonstrate limited biotechnology capabilities, but it is fragile outside a
controlled growth chamber and has a very limited functional lifetime due to
depletion of key metabolites, accumulation of metabolic waste, dehydration,
Significance
Environmental sensing typically
requires a separate transducer per
physicochemical target. Individual
sensors cannot respond to
unanticipated stimuli or repair
themselves when damaged. Fungal
mycelial networks respond to
chemical, optical, mechanical,
thermal, and biological inputs through
a single electrophysiological pathway,
but recording reliable signals from
living mycelium over operationally
relevant timescales has proven
difficult. Here, we develop a porous
bioceramic platform that sustains
fungal mycelium and records
extracellular voltages. We show that a
single device distinguishes 14
stimulus types, recovers
electrophysiological function within
72 h of mechanical damage, and
sustains calibration-quality signals
over long-term operation. Living
fungal networks can thus serve as
multimodal, self-repairing sensing
substrates when the stimulus space
and failure modes are not defined in
advance.

In such systems, viable operation is limited to days or
weeks, after which biological drift and stress artifacts
become difficult to separate from genuine signals as the
biodevice degrades over time and dehydrates (1, 14).
Platforms integrating living mycelium with an active
impedance interrogation array preserve viability and
demonstrate thermal sensing (15). However, they measure
a different signal class from the native extracellular voltage
and have been shown only for a single modality. More
broadly, the lack of a standardized and reproducible
recording method remains a major limitation in fungal
electrophysiology (1).
We present the MIND (Mycoponically Integrated
Network Device) platform, a dynamic multichannel extra-
cellular recording platform for living mycelial networks
(see Fig. 1). By integrating the growth and recording
systems, we advance the current state of the art through
two MIND architectures.
The MINDTube (Fig. 1D)
supports continuous mycelial growth on a cylindrical
bioceramic substrate with four differential circumferential
electrode channels, and the MINDPixel (Fig. 1E) is
designed to use discrete electrically isolated mycelial
“pixels” on flat bioceramic disks with localized electrode
pairs. These MIND systems sustained colonized Pleurotus
ostreatus mycelial networks, with extracellular recordings
for more than 11 months at the time of this submis-
sion. Using MINDTube, we characterize the response
characteristics of 14 input stimuli spanning the chemical,
optical, mechanical, thermal, and biological domains.
This was replicated in four additional fungal species
from different phylogenetic clades using MINDTube.
MINDPixel was also tested with visible white light as a
controlled model stimulus, and our experiments calibrate
morphology-specific intensity–response relationships and
decode stimulus location, duration, and continuous tra-
jectory from multichannel bioelectrical features. We also
demonstrate the MIND platform’s self-repair capabilities,
further substantiating the long-term viability and real-
world performance of these hybrid bioelectric devices.
Results
MIND provides stable passive readout across fourteen stimulus
classes. We characterized the MIND platform’s readout
by first confirming signal fidelity through abiotic controls,
then establishing the resting baseline, surveying responses
across fourteen stimulus classes, and documenting the
recharge behavior following repeated stimulation. Unless
otherwise noted, experiments used blue oyster mycelium
(Pleurotus ostreatus).
The substrate and electrode assembly produced no
stimulus-correlated artifacts. Bioceramic tubes without
mycelium were sterilized and exposed to all stimulus
classes used in this study, including chemical, optical,
mechanical, thermal, and biological stimuli, under an
acquisition protocol identical to that used in all biological
experiments.
No stimulus condition produced voltage
deflections above the noise floor.
For the biological
stimulus control, a maize leaf (Zea mays) was rendered
metabolically inert by isopropyl alcohol treatment and
24 hours of drying before placement adjacent to the sensor.
This condition also did not produce a measurable response.
Therefore, all reported signals required the living mycelial
layer.
With the mycelial network present, MIND produced a
resting potential that fluctuated around a slowly varying
mean (Fig. 1F). Median subtraction was applied before
all downstream analyses to center this baseline.
The
corrected signal provides the reference against which
stimulus-evoked responses are measured. Its properties re-
flect biophysical differences in electrophysiological activity
across fungal species.
Fourteen stimuli were applied to the MINDTube
without hardware modifications, each characterized across
30 independent events. The set spanned chemical (ace-
tone (CH3COCH3), isopropyl alcohol ((CH3)2CHOH),
carbon dioxide (CO2), propane (C3H8), smoke, and
MAP-Pro® gas (Worthington Industries, Inc.; 99.5%
propylene, C3H6; 0.5% propane, C3H8)), optical (white
visible light, near-infrared, UVB, and UVC), mechanical
(pressure, touch), thermal (temperature), and biological
(Phyllachora maydis tar spot spores) domains. Repre-
sentative single-stimulus responses are shown in Fig. 2A.
Modality-specific stimulus–response sweeps are illustrated
in Fig. 2B.
Each stimulus produced a measurable voltage deflection.
The response hierarchy was nonuniform (Fig. 2; Table 1).
Pressure produced the largest deflection, with ∆Vmax =
2.0 ± 1.3 mV and SNRmean = 15 ± 11. Tar spot disease
produced the second-largest amplitude (∆Vmax = 0.93 ±
0.15 mV) and the slowest recovery (τ1/e = 81 ± 55 s).
Recovery time constants spanned more than four orders
of magnitude across the full stimulus set. Peak amplitude,
mean signal-to-noise ratio, and τ1/e for each stimulus
are summarized in Table 1.
Response amplitude and
recovery kinetics differed systematically between stimulus
classes. Both features carry discriminative information
for downstream inference.
The mycelial network also resolves how a stimulus
is applied, not only its magnitude. Pressure, vacuum,
and carbon dioxide were each delivered at three loading
rates (pressure:
0.5, 2.0, 4.3 hPa s−1; vacuum:
0.16,
0.62, 1.30 hPa s−1; CO2:
11, 74, 188 ppm s−1) and
produced three distinguishable response families each,
indicating that the interface encodes stimulus rate as
well as magnitude. Pressure spanned 10.7–82.9 hPa and
reached end-of-range responses of 0.19 ± 0.01, 1.25 ± 0.20,
and 2.59 ± 0.21 mV across the slow, medium, and fast
rate curves. Vacuum spanned 4.2–22.8 hPa and reached
0.35±0.03, 0.51±0.05, and 1.41±0.12 mV. Carbon dioxide
showed the same rate-dependent structure over a proxy
range of 0.32–5.06 hPa, with end-of-range responses of
0.35 ± 0.02, 0.63 ± 0.03, and 0.88 ± 0.06 mV. IR and
isopropyl alcohol did not admit rate subdivision and
were treated as single-curve ranked-application stimuli.
IR increased across five ordered levels from 2.5 ± 0.17
to 7.1 ± 0.46 mV. Isopropyl alcohol increased across five

0.21 ± 0.016 to 0.64 ± 0.043 mV. Both curves showed a
concave saturating form, consistent with receptor satu-
ration shared across optical and chemical stimuli rather
than modality-specific saturation. The contrast between
rate-dependent mechanical and gas responses and receptor-
saturating optical and chemical responses is consistent

After repeated stimulation, the uncorrected baseline
exhibited a slow upward drift characteristic of mycelial
self-recharge (Fig. 2A). A linear model described this

Intensity Response Characterization. The fourteen-stimulus
survey established that amplitude and recovery kinetics
encode stimulus identity. We next quantify how much
information can be decoded from a single modality.
White visible light serves as the model stimulus because
intensity, timing, and spatial pattern are all independently
programmable. The experimental setups for both mor-
phologies are shown in Fig. 3A,B. All optical experiments
in this and the following two subsections were conducted
over approximately eight months of continuous platform
operation.
Morphology-specific calibration is required for reliable
intensity inference. Morphology selection alters the usable
operating range, not only physical geometry. We fit the
steady-state bioelectrical response of each morphology
with a Hill function.
Morphology-specific calibration
curves are shown in Fig. 3D,E. For MINDTube, the median
fit across 15 independent experiments was
fTube(ℓ) =
1.22 × ℓ0.94
5.40 0.94 + ℓ0.94 ,
R2 = 0.9981,
where ℓis light brightness (% of full LED output). The
near-unity exponent (n = 0.94) produces a near-linear
saturating regime.
MINDTube resolves fine intensity
differences at low illumination.
For MINDPixel, calibration across six independent
modules (18 experiments total) yielded the median fit
fPixel(ℓ) =
17.60 × ℓ3.90
115.64 3.90 + ℓ3.90 ,
R2 = 0.9303.
The steeper exponent (n = 3.90) produces a sigmoidal
transition. MINDPixel operates most sensitively in the
moderate-to-high illumination range. The two morpholo-
gies define complementary operating regimes for optical
intensity inference.
Amplitude structure encodes spatial and temporal features under
static illumination. With intensity calibrated, we asked what
spatial and temporal information the same signal carries.

Hyphal networks form electrically coupled lattices (1, 17).
Local perturbations should produce distributed responses
in which onset timing is shared across electrodes. Re-
sponse amplitude should remain graded by proximity to
the stimulus source. This predicts amplitude-based spatial
encoding instead of a time-of-flight code. We tested this
prediction across two flash paradigms (Fig. 3C).
For MINDTube, one to four walls were independently
illuminated for 1, 5, or 10 s.
Ridge regression on
multichannel baseline-corrected voltage features decoded
wall count at 59.5 ± 6.8%, stimulus duration class at
79.3 ± 5.9%, and wall identity at 73.2 ± 7.2%, across
three independent sessions and 21 experimental conditions
each repeated three times (Fig. 3F–H; SI Appendix,
Table S1). Wall count and wall identity are evaluated
against a four-class chance of 25%; duration decoding,
with three stimulus levels, is evaluated against a balanced
chance of 33.3%.
Duration decoding is the strongest
result. The temporal profile of the bioelectrical signal
encoded stimulus duration with high fidelity. The duration
confusion matrix (Fig. 3G) reflects a class distribution of
747, 29, and 42 trials for the 1 s, 5 s, and 10 s conditions.
Overall accuracy reached 96.8% (Cohen’s κ = 0.763); the
1 s condition comprising 91.3% of trials drives this figure,
and the balanced accuracy of 79.3% confirms performance
well above the 33.3% balanced chance across all three
classes. Wall-identity accuracy at 73.2%, nearly three
times the four-class chance, demonstrates that spatial
information is decodable.
Transient feature analysis confirmed the amplitude-
encoding hypothesis directly.

For MINDPixel, full-panel transition-direction classifi-

four spatially arranged MINDPixel units yielded 69.8 ±

Lagged decoding recovers continuous stimulus trajectory. Static
flashing demonstrated decodable spatial and temporal
structure in discrete stimulus states. Continuous tracking
requires the signal to follow a moving source across time.
We next sought to determine whether the same signal
can track a continuously moving one. Living networks
possess finite adaptation and recovery timescales (17–19).
Stimuli moving too slowly allow transient responses to
decay before new spatial information arrives.
Stimuli
moving too quickly prevent coherent entrainment before
the next cycle begins. Therefore, we aim to characterize
the natural temporal patterns for both morphologies here.
Two moving-stimulus paradigms are summarized in
Fig. 4. White-light bars rotated around MINDTube at
14, 6, and 1 deg s−1 across 33 independent sessions, with
lagged ridge regression as the best-performing decoder. A
vertical bar translated left to right across the MINDPixel
panel at 5, 10, and 15 px s−1 across 27 independent
sessions, decoded with the same lagged approach.
In
both cases, models incorporating recent signal history
outperformed instantaneous decoders.

For MINDPixel, position recovery improved monoton-

Discrete 4-bin accuracy improved from 36.8±6.2% without
contextual history to 51.5 ± 7.9% at eight history steps,
indicating that the fungal network retains positional state
over sub-second timescales.
The speed-dependent performance patterns across both
morphologies converge on a single conclusion that a
stimulus speed within each morphology’s operational
range maximizes decoding accuracy.
Two temporal
regimes underlie this behavior. Fast transients within
1 to 3 s of any stimulus change encode spatial information
through amplitude and slope differences.
A slower
sustained component encodes the intensity through the
Hill calibration.
Together, these regimes show that
fungal bioelectrical dynamics support inference about
continuously evolving environments.
Co-occurring stimuli produce partial superposition rather than com-
plete signal collapse. We next characterize platform behavior
when two stimuli are applied simultaneously. We analyzed
123 paired-stimulus events accumulated over ten months
of platform operation. Representative responses appear
in Fig. 5.
Inverse Fast Fourier Transformation (IFFT) features
yielded the best joint-bit accuracy of 0.285 ± 0.041. The
highest within-pair accuracy was 0.714 ± 0.063 for green
light paired with white visible light, with full pair-level
results in SI Appendix, Table S5. Weighted single-stimulus
template fits further confirmed the partial-superposition
structure, reaching R2 = 0.738 ± 0.082 for the best-fitting
pair.
Full-source separation from a merged channel is not
supported by these data. The above-chance decoding
indicates that co-occurring inputs are not collapsed into
an indistinguishable composite waveform. With the given
electrode geometry, simultaneous-stimulus responses are
best described as partial superposition, with separable
structure preserved alongside nonlinear coupling intro-
duced by shared downstream ionic machinery (1, 6).
Electrode geometry and channel selection influenced
separability under simultaneous stimulation.
These
findings define a practical ceiling that denser electrode
configurations may partially overcome.
Hill response structure generalizes across five phylogenetically
diverse fungal species. All of the preceding results were
obtained with blue oyster mycelium, so we next asked
whether the calibrated response structure extends to
other species. Core fungal electrophysiological machinery,
including photoreceptors, Ca2+ channels, and H+-ATPase,
is broadly conserved across fungal clades (4–6).
This
conservation predicts that a saturating Hill response
should be shared across species grown on the same
MIND interface. We cultivated four additional strains on
the MINDTubes, including reishi (Ganoderma lingzhi),
cordyceps (Cordyceps militaris), turkey tail (Trametes
versicolor), and lion’s mane (Hericium erinaceus), span-

All five strains produced Hill-function fits with R2 =

The bioceramic
platform supported consistent electrical coupling across
all five strains, functioning as a universal interface for
long-duration mycelial electrophysiology.
Inter-strain parameter variation confirmed that the
platform resolves species-specific differences in calibrated
sensitivity. Blue oyster and reishi produced the lowest
apparent threshold values (E = 6.75 and 6.97%); turkey
tail required the highest brightness before saturating
(E = 117.06%); cordyceps and lion’s mane occupied an
intermediate threshold but differed sharply in steepness
(n = 2.59 vs. 0.95).
These parameter differences are
consistent with strain-specific light-response biology re-
ported across these taxa (3, 20–24). Because E and n
are recoverable from calibration runs, strain selection
becomes a practical design parameter for matching device
sensitivity to a target illumination range.

capability of the mycelium on MIND modules, which other
existing hardware cannot support. To test autonomous
recovery, a 20 mm × 20 mm active mycelial region was
mechanically excised across three independent MIND-

Discussion
Living mycelial networks sustained on a mycoponic
bioceramic platform and coupled to passive extracellu-
lar recording function as calibrated multimodal sensing
substrates. Prior work in fungal electrophysiology has
established that mycelia generate stimulus-correlated
voltage changes, but those studies have been constrained
to operational windows of days to weeks, single-modality
demonstration, and qualitative signal interpretation (2,
8, 10, 11). MIND extends that work in three respects:
it sustains colonized mycelial networks for more than
11 months, it enables quantitative decoding of stimulus
identity, location, duration, and continuous trajectory,
and it supports autonomous repair of electrophysiological
function through the same bioceramic architecture that
provides long-term viability.
The latency-invariant, amplitude-based spatial encod-
ing recovered from MINDTube channels is consistent
with electrotonic propagation through the electrically
coupled hyphal lattice (1, 17). Locally applied stimuli
distribute rapidly across the network, producing near-
simultaneous voltage onsets at all recording channels
while encoding stimulus location in the spatial pattern of
response amplitude. Active illuminated walls produced
significantly larger peak amplitudes and steeper initial
slopes than inactive walls, while onset latency did not dif-
fer, supporting amplitude-based rather than latency-based
spatial coding. A secondary, slower modulation consistent
with Ca2+ buffering dynamics (17) carries additional
spatial information at longer timescales. Confirming the
underlying ionic mechanism will require pharmacological
block of Ca2+ channels and comparison of intact and
heat-inactivated mycelium.
The saturating Hill-type intensity response, conserved
across all five species with strain-specific fits of R2 = 0.89–
0.93, is consistent with finite receptor and transporter
capacity at the hyphal membrane (3, 6). The Hill exponent
varied systematically across morphologies, producing
complementary low-illumination (MINDTube, n = 0.94)
and moderate-to-high-illumination (MINDPixel, n = 3.90)
sensitivity regimes.
Cross-species conservation of this
response structure indicates that the Hill calibration
framework reflects core fungal electrophysiology rather
than a strain-specific artifact.
Inter-strain variation
in EC50 and Hill exponent may reflect divergence in
photoreceptor expression, membrane lipid composition,
or ecological light adaptation (4, 5). These parameters
can be selected to match target sensitivity requirements
without hardware modification, extending the platform’s
adaptability beyond a single fungal species.
Under simultaneous two-stimulus application, MIND
produces responses best described as partial superposition.
Above-chance joint-bit accuracy and high single-stimulus
template fit indicate that co-occurring inputs retain
separable structure in the bioelectrical output, consistent
with distinct upstream transduction pathways sharing
downstream ionic machinery (1, 6). Full source separation
was not achieved with the current four-channel geometry.
Additional mechanistic hypotheses, including spectral
discriminability from photoreceptor families with opposing
electrogenic coupling directions (26, 27) and opposing
baseline shifts from alcohol-induced membrane fluidiza-
tion (28), require genetic knockouts and narrowband
action spectra before they can be considered causal (1, 29).
The principal boundaries of the current implementation
are those of its electrode geometry and operational context
rather than those of the mycelium itself. Four differential
channels per MINDTube and four discrete pixels per
MINDPixel were sufficient to demonstrate multimodal
decoding and spatial inference in these proof-of-concept ar-
chitectures, but the mycelial network distributes stimulus-
evoked amplitude gradients at finer spatial scales than
this channel count can resolve.
Increasing electrode

density, while balancing nutrient delivery to the mycelium
layers, would improve spatial resolution and simultaneous
stimulation separability in parallel. The baseline drift
following repeated stimulation is small relative to the
smallest evoked deflections analyzed in our characteriza-
tion. Such small shifts are routinely handled by adaptive
baseline tracking. Periodic recalibration may be required
for long-duration deployments, especially under field
conditions. The 72-hour self-repair window represents a
genuine biological self-maintenance capability that scales
with nutrient availability and the severity of damage.
Its practical relevance depends on whether the target
application can tolerate a repair interval of that timescale,
which varies widely across deployment scenarios.
Overall, the results motivate two parallel tracks of
future work.
On the engineering side, higher-density
electrode arrays and tiled MINDPixel configurations
represent a path to improved spatial resolution and
simultaneous-stimulus separability, as mycelium already
encodes stimulus information at finer spatial scales than
the current four-channel geometry can sample. On the
biological side, strain selection represents an additional
design dimension that can be matched to target modalities
and sensitivity requirements before fabrication, with the
EC50 and Hill-exponent variation reported here as a
practical tuning parameter. Beyond these performance di-
mensions, the primary sensing element of MIND is a living
fungal network composed of biodegradable biopolymers
cultivated on a kiln-fired ceramic substrate. Whether
these material properties translate into a quantifiable
lifecycle advantage over conventional solid-state sensor
suites covering equivalent stimulus domains remains
an open question that a full comparative assessment,
accounting for nutrient medium production, ceramic firing,
and operational power draw alongside fabrication inputs,
would need to address.
Materials and Methods
Mycoponic Bioceramic Platform. The bioceramic substrate was engi-
neered to act as a mechanic filter that is antiomicrobial highly porous to
support long-term mycelial viability (16). A powder blend (wt. %: 30 china
clay, 30 ball clay, 15 CaCO3, 25 diatomaceous earth) was sieved, dispersed
in water with a polyacrylate dispersant and a cellulose-ether binder, and
vacuum de-aired before forming. For the MINDTube morphology, the slurry
was pressure-extruded to L = 90 mm, OD = 50 mm, wall thickness
t = 7 mm, and fired at 1100◦C. The fired body exhibited a median pore
size of approximately 0.3 µm, providing mechanical exclusion for most
bacteria. Fluid-port end pieces were press-fitted to each end face for
gravity-fed nutrient delivery. For the MINDPixel morphology, the substrate
was formed as a flat ceramic disk of 30 mm radius and 4 mm thickness. Key
geometry and electrode dimensions for both morphologies are summarized
in Fig. 1.
Electrode Fabrication and Integration. Electrodes were fabricated as
a copper-Kapton laminate. Copper tape was uniformly spray-inked and
laser-scribed into 80 mm × 1.5 mm rectangular traces, then processed by
standard wet chemical etching. Kapton insulation tape was precision-cut
using a CNC machine. The laminated electrodes were transferred onto the
bioceramic surface using a positioning guide, with Kapton covering the full
trace length except for a 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm exposed copper contact pad at
the sensing interface.
For MINDTube, four electrode pairs were placed equidistantly around
the outer circumference, positioned 70 mm axially along the lower portion
of the tube where fruiting bodies concentrate; each pair formed one
differential recording channel.
For MINDPixel, each pixel carried one
localized differential interface, so a four-pixel arrangement yielded four
simultaneously recorded channels. Copper forms a self-limiting oxide layer
(Cu2O) that stabilizes rapidly; once colonized, the mycelium grows over
the contact pad, further limiting oxidative exposure. Baseline electrode
coupling remained stable across weeks of continuous operation throughout
all reported experiments.
Inoculation and Cultivation. Assembled bioceramic modules were steril-
ized by autoclaving and inoculated with mycelial liquid culture of blue oyster
mycelium (Pleurotus ostreatus) as the primary experimental strain (16).
Similarly, other strains were also innoculated onto the autoclaved tubes
and fed with MNM v3, with growth proceeding for approximately two weeks
under low light (< 50 lux), high moisture (70–90% relative humidity), and
cool ambient laboratory conditions (18–22◦C) until stable colonization was
established. During operation, a custom nutrient blend based on Mycoponic
Nutrient Medium V2 was gravity-fed via the fluid-port end piece (MINDTube)
or through a sealed chamber reservoir (MINDPixel), from which nutrients
diffused through the porous ceramic to sustain the mycelial layer. For multi-
strain experiments, four additional species were cultivated on the same
platform: reishi (Ganoderma lingzhi), cordyceps (Cordyceps militaris),
turkey tail (Trametes versicolor), and lion’s mane (Hericium erinaceus).
Additional details on the mycoponics materials and protocols are described
in Porterfield et al. (16).
Signal Acquisition and Stimulus Delivery. Bioelectrical signals were
acquired with an ADS1263-based 32-bit delta-sigma conversion chain
operated in differential mode at 400 SPS per channel using the con-
verter’s internal 2.5 V reference. Stimulus control and electrophysiological
acquisition shared the same Raspberry Pi controller and software time
base, ensuring precise alignment between stimulus delivery and voltage
recording.
MINDTube experiments used four simultaneous differential
channels; MINDPixel experiments used one channel per pixel, with four
channels recorded simultaneously for full four-pixel configurations.
A 20 s baseline segment was recorded at the start of each session.
Local baseline subtraction and moving-mean smoothing were applied
before feature extraction and decoding. Detailed preprocessing parameters,
circuit diagrams, and source-control scripts are provided in the SI Appendix.
Optical stimuli were delivered as electromagnetic radiation using a
programmable 64 × 64 RGB LED matrix for the blue-light (λ ≈470 nm),
green-light (λ ≈525 nm), and white visible-light (approximately 400–
700 nm) conditions, together with auxiliary near-infrared (IR; λ ≈850 nm),
ultraviolet B (UVB; λ ≈311 nm), and ultraviolet C (UVC; λ ≈254 nm)
sources.
For MINDTube, four LED panels arranged around the tube
circumference enabled independent wall illumination and continuous
rotation of light bars.
For MINDPixel, a single panel was positioned
directly above the disk. Programmed LED output percentage served as
the ground-truth intensity reference for all calibration experiments, with
0% corresponding to LED off and 100% to full programmed panel output.
Ambient visible-light level was monitored with a VEML7700 ambient-light
sensor; visible and IR optical output was verified with a TSL2591 light-to-
digital sensor. UVB source output was verified with a VEML6075 UV sensor,
and UVC source output was verified with a filtered 254 nm photodiode
(S12742-254).
The stimulus bank encompassed chemical stimuli (acetone, isopropyl
alcohol, carbon dioxide (CO2), propane, MAP-Pro gas (primarily propy-
lene/propene, C3H6)), optical stimuli (white visible light, IR, UVB, and
UVC), mechanical stimuli (touch and pressure loading), thermal stimuli
(temperature), and biological perturbations (tar spot of maize caused by
Phyllachora maydis). Detailed source specifications, chamber geometries,
and timing schedules are provided in the SI Appendix.
For stimuli admitting controlled delivery, chamber conditions were
monitored continuously with environmental and stimulus-specific trans-
ducers. Pressure, vacuum, chamber temperature, and relative humidity
were monitored with a BME680 environmental sensor. CO2 concentration
was monitored with an SCD41 CO2 sensor. Propane-rich gas exposure
was monitored with a TGS2610-D00 LP-gas sensor; the same sensor
served as a chamber-exposure proxy during MAP-Pro welding gas trials.
Delivery rate was set with a mass-flow-controlled feed and verified against
the commanded setpoint throughout each application window. Within each
rate group, the instantaneous rate of change was derived from the corre-
sponding sensor time series and used to construct response envelopes for
pressure, vacuum, and gas-exposure sweeps. Environmental variables not
under direct manipulation, including ambient room temperature (20–24◦C),
relative humidity (40–60%), and background light level (<50 lux during
optical sessions; 200–400 lux during non-optical sessions), were monitored
throughout and maintained within these bounds to ensure that observed
bioelectrical responses reflected the intended stimulus class.
Experimental Units and Replication. A device denotes one living
MINDTube or one living MINDPixel unit. A session denotes one continuous
recording run on one device under one defined experimental protocol. An

Self-Repair Protocol. A 20 mm × 20 mm region of the active mycelial
surface was mechanically excised and the ceramic chamber was filled with
nutrient feed prior to excision to support regrowth. Recovery was monitored
over seven days by flashing a concentrated light beam for 5 s onto the
damaged area every 30 minutes and recording the maximum response
amplitude. Recovery was assessed against three criteria: complete re-
coverage by visual inspection, restoration of baseline electrical activity, and
maintained responsiveness to stimulation.
Tar Spot of Maize Exposure. A sealed chamber was sprayed with
isopropyl alcohol, then hydrogen peroxide, and placed in a UVC sterilization
chamber for 24 hours. Harvested maize leaves (Zea mays) carrying tar
spot lesions caused by Phyllachora maydis were then placed inside the
chamber containing an active MIND device, and the bioelectrical response
was recorded under the standard acquisition protocol.
